fixes.explanation: Shepherd, friend! Peter says, “you were like sheep going astray,” but now “you have returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls.” (1 Peter 2:25) Sheep going astray, then back to the Shepherd. That's a good place to land at the end.

I see why you'd go there, since Peter mentions slander in the very next verse. But in verse 11 Peter names something else. He says the desires of the flesh are what war against the soul. Fear of people never shows up in that line, friend.
Glorify, friend! Peter says the people slandering them may see the good deeds and glorify God “…on the day He visits us.” (1 Peter 2:12) Good deeds do the talking, and God gets the glory.

Blame is what slanderers are busy handing out, so I get the pull. But Peter says they may see the good deeds and glorify God. The word in that blank turns the whole verse upside down. Blame is out and glory is in.
Forget isn't in this verse at all, friend. Peter says the good deeds are there for the slanderers to see, so that they may glorify God. The day Peter names is the day He visits us.
Close to the neighborhood, since Peter does mention the king and governors. But the verse says to submit for the Lord's sake, not the nation's. The Lord is the reason Peter gives, friend.

That's it, friend. Peter says the governors are sent by the king “…to punish those who do wrong and to praise those who do right.” (1 Peter 2:14) Two jobs, and they go in both directions. Praising those who do right is half of what they're sent for, and that's right there in the text.
By doing good, friend. Peter says it's God's will that “…by doing good you should silence the ignorance of foolish men.” (1 Peter 2:15) Doing good is the way Peter names for silencing that ignorance.
Packing up sounds tempting some days. But Peter never tells them to move. He says doing good is how the ignorance of foolish men gets silenced.

That's it, friend. Peter says, “But if you suffer for doing good and you endure it, this is commendable before God.” (1 Peter 2:20) He sets it right beside being beaten for doing wrong. The one he calls commendable is suffering for doing good and enduring it.
Peter never mentions how long the suffering lasts. He says suffering for doing good and enduring it is commendable before God. The length isn't the point, friend, the reason is.

Nice try, but secrets don't show up in this verse. Peter's contrast is between being beaten for doing wrong and suffering for doing good. What he calls commendable before God is suffering for doing good and enduring it. Whether anybody knows isn't the question, friend.

It's True, friend. Peter says of Jesus, “He committed no sin, and no deceit was found in His mouth.” (1 Peter 2:22) Nothing is hiding in His record. That's the One whose footsteps they're told to follow.

Gently is a sweet word, but Peter doesn't use it here. He says Jesus entrusted Himself to Him who judges justly. Gentle is about how kindly something is done, while just is about getting it right. Jesus put Himself in the hands of the One who judges justly, friend.

Return does show up in this passage, but later, in verse 25, where the believers have returned to the Shepherd. In verse 24 the word is die. Peter says Jesus bore our sins so that we might die to sin and live to righteousness. Right passage, different verse, friend.
